summary: United States conventions. A one-page resume is the norm early in a career; an academic CV is a different document entirely and is supported separately.

photo.note: A photo on a US resume is strongly discouraged: it creates a risk of discrimination claims, so many employers discard applications that include one. It is off by default.

personalInfo.note: US resumes carry no date of birth, marital status, gender, nationality or photo. Exceptions: a work-authorisation statement is common, and an address is usually just city and state.

page.note: One page for under ten years of experience; two pages thereafter. Recruiters spend seconds on a first pass, and length is not rewarded.

notes: US employers are the heaviest users of applicant tracking systems. Multi-column layouts, tables, text boxes, images and headers/footers are actively risky here.
Dates should be unambiguous: MM/YYYY avoids the DD/MM versus MM/DD ambiguity entirely.
Use the exact job title from the advert as the headline where it is accurate — keyword matching is literal.
US resumes use terse, achievement-first bullets with no personal pronouns — "Led a team of six", not "I led a team of six".
Present tense for the current role, past tense for previous ones.
Spelling should be consistent US English (organization, analyze, program).

advisories.text: Resume bullets typically open with an action verb and omit "I"; this is a strong US convention.
US recruiters expect measurable outcomes. Where you know a number, include it; where you do not, describe the outcome without inventing one.
"References available upon request" is not needed and is generally omitted.
If you need sponsorship or already have work authorisation, stating it briefly near the top removes a common early-screening question.
